description: We’re Team DuduBubu, and we built Jezero Go/No-Go, a Marswalk planner using real NASA terrain of Jezero Crater. Pick your science sites, see if the crew can make it home in time, then run the walk. When Mission Control cuts the clock halfway out, you decide what’s still worth it.
summary: Jezero Go/No-Go is an interactive Marswalk planner for western Jezero Crater, designed like a printed mission planning sheet. Visitors plan a walk to science sites across a topographic chart built from the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's CTX elevation model, with Perseverance Mastcam-Z photos of each site. The planner computes terrain-aware routes live in the browser: walking speed changes with slope, so the trip back takes a different time from the trip out. It gives a GO or NO-GO against the time limit, marks the point of no return, and hatches the area the crew can't reach and still get home from. Then visitors run the EVA. When Mission Control cuts the clock halfway out, they choose to continue, re-plan to closer sites or turn back. This answers the challenge by layering real NASA terrain and rover data into one view that helps a human explorer plan a safe Marswalk, and it shows how terrain, time and science priorities shape a real go/no-go decision.
details:
Jezero Go/No-Go is an interactive Marswalk planner for western Jezero Crater, designed like a printed mission planning sheet.

How it works: the crew starts at a simulated habitat. Visitors pick science sites, including their own sites clicked anywhere on the chart, and give each a science value. The planner computes terrain-aware routes live in the browser. Walking speed depends on slope, so climbs are slower and the trip back takes a different time from the trip out. It finds the fastest visiting order and gives a GO or NO-GO against the time limit: the Mission Control budget or the suit's life support, whichever is shorter, minus a 10-minute reserve. For a NO-GO plan the chart marks the point of no return, the first spot where the fastest way home would arrive too late. Red hatching covers the area the crew could not reach and still return from. "Best plan" picks the most valuable set of sites that still fits.

Then visitors run the EVA. At an unexpected moment Mission Control cuts 30 minutes. The planner recalculates from the crew's current position and offers three choices: continue, re-plan to the most valuable remaining sites, or turn back now, each with its new return time. With the default settings the west fan takes 141 minutes against a 150-minute safe return; after the cut it becomes NO-GO, and the crater floor (84 minutes) is the plan that fits. A guided tour shows the whole flow without any clicks, and the chart works with the keyboard and on phones.

Tools: Python, Rasterio, NumPy and Pillow turn the USGS CTX elevation mosaic into a relief basemap and a compact elevation grid. The app uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Canvas, with no backend. Routing runs Dijkstra's algorithm over each cell's eight neighbours, costed by walking time from Tobler's hiking function. The planner tries every visiting order and every subset of sites, and a browser test page checks the engine.

Creativity: the look borrows from printed survey charts and mission paperwork: paper and ink colours with one Mars-red accent, contour lines every 10 m, numbered planning sections and a stamped GO/NO-GO verdict.

Benefits and impact: it turns real NASA terrain and rover data into a decision people can feel, showing how terrain, time and science priorities shape a go/no-go call on Mars. Factors we considered: astronaut safety margins, the difference between outbound and return times, suit limits, changing plans mid-mission, and accessibility. Limits: Tobler's function is an Earth hiking model, and the habitat and site positions are illustrative. It is an educational tool, not an operational planner.
